title: From Street Food Vendors to Italian Nonnas: How Indian Wedding Menus Became Personal
excerpt: The grand 100-dish buffet is giving way to curated, story-driven menus — couples are flying in favourite chaatwallas, recreating first-date dishes, and turning wedding meals into edible biographies.
body:
• Indian wedding food is shifting from massive 100-dish buffets to curated, story-driven menus where every dish reflects the couple's personal history, regional roots, or travel experiences.
  • The 'micro concept' trend sees families bringing in specialists — from street food vendors to international restaurant chefs — rather than relying on a single caterer for everything.
  • Lesser-known regional cuisines like Bihari, Manipuri, and Chettinad are increasingly requested alongside international options such as Peruvian and Thai.
  • Destination weddings are accelerating the trend, with couples drawing from the culinary identity of their celebration location.

The End of the Mega Buffet

For decades, the Indian wedding was measured by the length of its buffet — metres of chafing dishes, dozens of cuisines, sheer volume as a statement of hospitality. That era is fading. "The days of having 100 dishes, metres and metres of long buffets are long gone," says celebrity chef and restaurateur Ritu Dalmia, co-owner of DIVA Catering. "Today it is all about less is more."

In its place, a different philosophy has taken hold: food as storytelling. Couples are building wedding menus around the places they have lived, the dishes that mark their relationship milestones, and the regional cuisines of their families. The result is meals designed not just to feed guests but to narrate.

The Rise of the Micro Concept

One of the biggest shifts in luxury wedding catering is the move toward what the industry calls 'micro concepts' — specialized food experiences built around a single chef, restaurant, cuisine, or iconic dish. Instead of asking one caterer to attempt 30 cuisines, families are bringing in specialists known for doing one thing exceptionally well.

Dalmia has taken the idea to striking lengths. For a wedding in Udaipur earlier this year, she flew in grandmothers from Puglia in southern Italy to make handmade pasta. "They did not speak a word of English," she recalls. "But they won the hearts of everyone." For another celebration in Marrakech, she collaborated with acclaimed Peruvian chef Pia León of Kjolle, Bangkok's Bo.lan, and pastry chef Renne Frank.

"The brief earlier was 'impress them,' now it's 'move them.'"

— Sanjay Vazirani, Founder, Foodlink Luxury Catering

Foodlink Luxury Catering, which has handled the Deepika Padukone-Ranveer Singh and Anant Ambani-Radhika Merchant celebrations, reports similar demand. Clients now ask for recreations of a specific city's street food legend, royal Thai counters, and live patisserie experiences.

Street Food Goes Luxe

The Ambani wedding celebrations in 2024 put the trend on full display. Varanasi's Kashi Chaat Bhandar was flown to Mumbai for their iconic tamatar chaat. Jaipur's Pandit Ji Vade Wale and Indore's JMB Catering brought their signature dahi vadas and garadu chaat.

Such requests have become common, according to Foodlink's Vazirani. Families insist on bringing their favourite vada pav stall from their college days, the halwai their grandmother swore by, or a dish from their own neighbourhood. The challenge lies in scaling flavours from a few hundred servings to thousands without losing authenticity.

A Menu of Memories

At Mumbai's Sage & Saffron, couples start the planning process by answering a simple question: what role has food played in their relationship? One couple's love of South Indian breakfasts and Thailand holidays became Chettinad-style prawns finished with a lemongrass glaze. Another couple's rainy-day ritual of eating bhutta on a drive was transformed into baby corn with corn mousse and chilli salt.

Chef Manu Chandra of Single Thread designed a multi-course dinner for a Chennai couple that traced every city they had lived in — from a favourite momo shop to Singapore's hawker stalls. "People will carry that for a long, long time," Chandra says. "There is greater memory association and more tangibility in what the event was all about."

Where It's Heading

Destination weddings are accelerating the movement. According to Sage & Saffron, couples increasingly draw from the culinary identity of the place where they are celebrating — a Rajasthan wedding might feature a local kachori specialist, while a Kerala celebration showcases dosas and rasam from a beloved institution.

The abundance of the Indian wedding is not disappearing. But the question has changed. It is no longer about how much food a wedding can offer, but what that food has to say.
nri_angle: Diaspora weddings are at the forefront of this trend, with NRI couples drawing on cuisines from countries they have lived in and foods that trace their cross-cultural journeys.
author: Diaspora Desk
